findings.title: Backup-code login skips password verification when any totpCode is also sent
findings.body:
The password is only checked when `user.password && !credentials.totpCode` (line 121). The new backup-code branch is evaluated before the TOTP branch and only needs `credentials.backupCode` to be truthy.

An attacker can POST to the credentials callback with `email`, any `password`, any non-empty `totpCode` (e.g. "1") and a valid `backupCode`. Because a totpCode is present, the password check is skipped. The backup-code branch then accepts the request without ever looking at the TOTP value.

The result is that a single leaked backup code plus the user's email is enough to take over the account. The codes are typically saved in the downloaded `cal-backup-codes.txt` or on the clipboard. This defeats the purpose of a *second* factor.

Fix: always verify the password when a backup code is used, or check the password based on identity provider rather than on whether `totpCode` is present.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write lets a backup code be reused and can resurrect consumed codes
findings.body:
The code consumes a backup code by:
1. reading `user.backupCodes`,
2. decrypting and finding the index in memory,
3. writing back the re-encrypted array.

There is no transaction, optimistic version check or conditional update.

Two concurrent login requests with the same code will both pass validation and both succeed, which breaks the documented "each backup code can be used exactly once" guarantee. Two concurrent logins with *different* codes will each write their own snapshot. The later write overwrites the earlier one, so a consumed code becomes valid again (lost update).

Use an atomic conditional update (e.g. `updateMany` where `backupCodes` equals the value read, retrying on 0 rows) or a row lock inside a transaction.

findings.title: Backup code match is case- and whitespace-sensitive while UI suggests uppercase
findings.body:
Codes are generated as lowercase hex (`crypto.randomBytes(5).toString("hex")`). The comparison only strips dashes (`replaceAll("-", "")`) and then does an exact `indexOf`. The input placeholder is `XXXXX-XXXXX`, which implies uppercase entry.

A user who types the code in uppercase, or pastes it with surrounding whitespace, gets `IncorrectBackupCode` even though the code is valid. The same issue exists in `disable.ts` line 61.

Normalize with `.trim().toLowerCase()` before comparing.

findings.title: Dismissing the backup-codes step via ESC/overlay leaves UI showing 2FA as disabled
findings.body:
After a successful `enable` call, the modal now switches to `DisplayBackupCodes` instead of calling `onEnable()`. `onEnable` is only invoked from the "Close" button.

If the user dismisses the dialog with ESC or by clicking outside, `onOpenChange` fires instead. The parent just toggles `open`, so its `enabled` state is never set and `viewer.me` is never invalidated. The settings switch therefore shows 2FA as off even though it is enabled server-side.

The component's `step` state also stays at `DisplayBackupCodes`. Clicking the switch again reopens the modal on the backup-codes screen instead of the enable flow.

Call `onEnable` (or equivalent state sync) when the modal is closed from this step, or handle it in `onOpenChange`.

findings.title: Copy button reports success unconditionally and crashes when Clipboard API is unavailable
findings.body:
The result of `navigator.clipboard.writeText(...)` is neither awaited nor caught, and the success toast is shown immediately. If the write is rejected (for example, no permission), the user is told the codes were copied when they were not, and they may close the only screen that ever shows the codes.

On self-hosted instances served over plain HTTP (non-localhost), `navigator.clipboard` is `undefined`. The handler then throws a TypeError and nothing is copied.

Await the promise and show an error toast on failure.

findings.title: "missing_backup_codes" tells users to generate codes in settings, but no such feature exists
findings.body:
The message reads "No backup codes found. Please generate them in your settings." This PR adds no way to generate or regenerate backup codes. They are only created in `setup.ts`, which refuses to run when 2FA is already enabled.

This matters in two cases:
- Users who enabled 2FA before this migration have `backupCodes = null`. They get this message and cannot follow it except by disabling and re-enabling 2FA.
- Users who exhaust all 10 codes have an array of `null`s. They get `incorrect_backup_code` rather than any guidance.

Either add a regenerate flow or reword the message to the actual remedy.

findings.title: tabIndex=-1 on shared PasswordField toggle removes keyboard access to show/hide password
findings.body:
Adding `tabIndex={-1}` to the visibility toggle button in the shared `PasswordField` makes the show/hide control unreachable by keyboard. This applies to every password field in the app, not just the 2FA modals.

This is an accessibility regression for keyboard and screen-reader users, and it is unrelated to the backup-code feature.

findings.title: Backup codes stored reversibly encrypted rather than hashed
findings.body:
Backup codes are only ever compared for equality and never need to be shown again after setup. Even so, they are stored with `symmetricEncrypt` using the app-wide `CALENDSO_ENCRYPTION_KEY`.

Anyone who obtains a DB dump plus that key can recover every user's unused backup codes in plaintext. Hashing each code (as is done for passwords) would avoid this. The TOTP secret has to be reversible, but backup codes do not.

findings.title: No tests for logging in or disabling 2FA with a backup code; enable test asserts nothing
findings.body:
The new authentication paths have no tests:
- backup-code login in `next-auth-options.ts`;
- backup-code disable in `disable.ts`;
- one-time consumption of a code.

The PR leaves a TODO for these instead.

In the first test, `expect(page.locator(...).isChecked()).toBeTruthy()` passes a Promise to `expect`, so it always passes, as the added FIXME admits. The test also navigates to logout without waiting for the enable request or the new backup-codes screen, so it can race.

The copy test only waits for the toast, which is shown regardless of whether the clipboard write succeeded.
